sec: Alkaline phosphatase & cholestasis · sources, duct dilation and delta bilirubin

items.q: What is the normal reference range for serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP), and what level signifies cholestasis?
opts: Normal: 40–140 U/L; Cholestasis: >4 times normal (>560 U/L)
Normal: 10–50 U/L; Cholestasis: >2 times normal (>100 U/L)
Normal: 100–300 U/L; Cholestasis: >10 times normal (>1000 U/L)
Normal: 20–80 U/L; Cholestasis: >3 times normal (>240 U/L)
items.exp: Normal ALP is 40–140 U/L, and levels > 4 times normal (>560 U/L) indicate cholestasis. (Book p990)

items.q: Why is serum alkaline phosphatase paradoxically decreased in Wilson's disease?
opts: Excess copper displaces zinc, an essential co-factor required for ALP structure and function
Direct transcriptional inhibition of the canalicular ALP gene by copper toxicity
Accelerated urinary clearance of ALP via proximal tubular Fanconi syndrome
Denaturation of circulating ALP by systemic hemolytic free radicals
items.exp: In Wilson's disease, serum ALP decreases because copper displaces zinc, an essential co-factor for alkaline phosphatase. (Book p990)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a physiological tissue source of Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)?
items.exp: The sources of ALP listed are Liver (canalicular membrane), Bone, Intestine, Kidney, and Placenta; skeletal muscle is not a source. (Book p990)

items.q: Match each cholestatic enzyme marker with its tissue origin — 1) GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase) 2) 5'-nucleotidase … A) Originates from both liver and bone B) Originates exclusively from the liver
items.exp: GGT is specific to the liver ('Source: Only liver'), whereas 5'-nucleotidase originates from both liver and bone. (Book p990)

items.q: An isolated elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase is identified on routine health screening. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm whether the ALP elevation is of hepatic origin?
opts: Serum gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) and abdominal ultrasound (USG)
items.exp: To confirm hepatic origin of raised ALP, serum GGT and abdominal ultrasound (USG) are performed. (Book p990)

items.q: A 36-year-old woman presents with severe generalized pruritus and jaundice. Her direct bilirubin is >50% of total, ALP is 680 U/L (>4x normal), and GGT is markedly elevated. Abdominal ultrasonography reveals completely normal intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts without dilation. What is the diagnosis?
opts: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas
items.exp: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with ALP > 4x normal, raised GGT, and normal duct caliber on USG defines intrahepatic cholestasis. (Book p990)

items.q: Fill up: In intrahepatic cholestasis, the prominent clinical symptom of pruritus is primarily caused by the systemic accumulation of ______.
items.exp: Pruritus in intrahepatic cholestasis is due to bile acid accumulation in tissues. (Book p990)

items.q: Which of the following is NOT listed under intrahepatic cholestasis causes on this page?
items.exp: Causes of intrahepatic cholestasis listed are Drugs, Cholangitis (Primary Biliary, Primary Sclerosing), Sarcoid, and Sepsis; duct dilation indicates extrahepatic cholestasis. (Book p990)

items.q: In a patient presenting with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, ALP > 4x normal, and elevated GGT, abdominal ultrasound reveals prominent biliary duct dilation. What is the next management step?
opts: Referral to surgeon for surgical or endoscopic relief of obstruction
Initiation of oral ursodeoxycholic acid and outpatient follow-up
Prescription of topical emollients and antihistamines for pruritus
items.exp: Biliary duct dilation on USG indicates extrahepatic cholestasis (obstruction), for which the management flowchart specifies: 'Refer to surgeon'. (Book p990)

items.q: What is the elimination half-life (T1/2) of free conjugated bilirubin compared to the delta bilirubin (conjugated bilirubin covalently bound to albumin) complex?
opts: Free conjugated bilirubin: 4 hours; Delta bilirubin complex: 14–21 days
Free conjugated bilirubin: 24 hours; Delta bilirubin complex: 48 hours
Free conjugated bilirubin: 10 days; Delta bilirubin complex: 30 days
Free conjugated bilirubin: 1 hour; Delta bilirubin complex: 7 days
items.exp: Free conjugated bilirubin has a half-life of 4 hours, whereas delta bilirubin (bound covalently to albumin) has a half-life of 14–21 days. (Book p990)

items.q: Assess the two statements on delta bilirubin: I Delta bilirubin forms when conjugated bilirubin binds irreversibly and covalently to albumin. II Delta bilirubin is rapidly cleared by the kidneys within 4 hours.
items.exp: Statement I is true because conjugated bilirubin binds irreversibly and covalently to albumin. Statement II is false because delta bilirubin has a prolonged half-life of 14–21 days matching albumin. (Book p990)
